title: Sell Mineral Rights in Price, UT
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Price, UT | Carbon County Seat
metaDescription: Own mineral rights in Price, UT, the Carbon County seat? We research recorder records and buy coal, gas, and CBM interests with a patient cash offer.
heroLead: Price is the Carbon County seat, which means every mineral deed, probate order, and lease affecting this part of the coal country runs through the recorder's office a few blocks off Main Street.
intro: Carbon County was built on coal, and Price grew up as the commercial hub for a string of mining towns strung along Highway 6 and the rail line. Mineral ownership here often reflects that history directly: interests carved out generations ago when a coal company bought the surface but reserved or purchased the coal separately, leaving heirs today holding gas or oil rights under ground where someone else owns the coal.

Because Price is the county seat, we typically can confirm your chain of title faster here than in smaller Carbon County towns, since everything is on file in one courthouse rather than scattered across older township records.

sections.heading: A courthouse town with layered mineral history
paragraphs: The Carbon County recorder's office holds records going back to the original coal-era patents, and a Price-area mineral interest can involve several distinct severances on the same tract: surface, coal, and oil and gas often owned by three different parties. We pull the full chain before we make an offer, so you're not guessing what you actually hold.

This matters especially for interests that passed through probate without a formal mineral deed. If your grandparents' estate never specifically itemized the mineral rights, they may still be intact and transferable, just undocumented in a way that needs a title search to confirm.

sections.heading: Coal, coalbed methane, and conventional gas
paragraphs: Price sits near the transition between the Ferron coal fairway to the south and older conventional gas fields to the north and west, so interests here can be tied to any combination of coal royalty, coalbed methane, and conventional production depending on the specific section. We ask for your legal description early precisely because two tracts a mile apart can have completely different production histories.
Legacy coal royalties, where they still exist, tend to be small and steady; gas royalties from newer wells swing more with commodity prices and well performance.

sections.heading: How the sale works
paragraphs: Send us a deed, probate order, or check stub and the legal description, and we'll confirm your interest against the Carbon County recorder's records ourselves. We'll walk you through what we found, make an offer, and if you accept, we handle the closing paperwork and file the conveyance with the county.
There's no obligation at the offer stage, and we're comfortable if you want a second opinion before deciding.

faqs.question: My family's estate never mentioned mineral rights. Do we still own them?
faqs.answer: Possibly. Minerals often pass through probate implicitly along with the rest of an estate even when not itemized. A title search of the Carbon County records will confirm what actually transferred.

faqs.question: Is coal royalty worth more or less than gas royalty here?
faqs.answer: It depends on the specific lease and production. Legacy coal royalties tend to be smaller and steadier, while gas royalties vary more with well performance and current prices. We value each on its own numbers.

faqs.question: How long does the title search take before I get an offer?
faqs.answer: For Price interests, usually a matter of days, since the Carbon County recorder's records are centralized and organized compared to some smaller jurisdictions.
